From this we learn the folly of hoping to gain from this world a satisfying good, and the true wisdom of going to God for blessedness.

title: Ecclesiastes 2:12
text:
To behold wisdom, and madness, and folly; to compare them together. The Preacher had found both earthly wisdom and folly to be vanity, and he now inquires what advantage the former has over the latter. 
 
  For what can the man do; as much as to say, None can be more competent to make this comparison; for who that comes after me in this inquiry will be able to add any thing new to my experience? 
 
  Cometh after the king; cometh after a king like me in this investigation.

title: Ecclesiastes 2:13
text: Wisdom excelleth folly; in its proper nature.

title: Ecclesiastes 2:14
text:
Are in his head; where he can use them to good purpose.  This is the superiority of wisdom over folly. 
 
  One event happeneth to them all; wise men and fools are alike subject to suffering and death; so that here, wisdom has no advantage over folly.  We must carefully remember that he is speaking of the earthly advantages of wisdom.  Compare the words of the apostle: "If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable."   I Corinthians 15:19

title: Ecclesiastes 2:15
text: Since wisdom, the most excellent of all earthly possessions, cannot exempt men from suffering, disappointment, and death, which are also the lot of fools, it is manifest that God designs this world to be a place of trial for men, and not their final portion.  It is only when we thus regard and use it, that it ceases to be vanity.

title: Ecclesiastes 2:18
text:
Labor; estate accumulated by labor. 
 
  Because I should leave it; another sad disadvantage under which the wise man labors.  He must leave all his estate to his successor, who may be a fool--as Rehoboam, Solomon's son, actually was in comparison with his father.

title: Ecclesiastes 2:24
text:
Nothing better for a man; that is, nothing better to be gained from his earthly toil.  When he enjoys it with a cheerful and contented spirit, he makes the most of it. 
 
  This also; the capacity thus to enjoy the fruits of our labor. 
 
It is our duty and privilege to receive with glad and thankful hearts the gifts of God's providence, and to enjoy them without anxious thought for the morrow.  Thus we gain from them all the good which they are capable of yielding.  But unless we lift our hearts upwards from the gifts to God the infinite Giver, we shall find that "this also is vanity and vexation of spirit."

title: Ecclesiastes 2:25
text: Can hasten hereunto; can ardently engage in the enjoyment of worldly good.  He confirms what he has just said by an appeal to his own experience, which was as full as any man's could be.

title: Ecclesiastes 2:26
text: This also is vanity; what has been said of enjoying one's labor. It is the most that one can gain from it, yet it is unsatisfying.

title: Ecclesiastes 3:1
text:
vv 1-9. 
 
  To every thing there is a season--wherein he laboreth; in human affairs there is, by God's appointment, a constant alternation of opposite events, lying beyond the control of men.  For the purposes of probation, this is a wise and good arrangement.  But for the enjoyment of this world, which is what the Preacher has in view, it is an evil; for it makes all present good uncertain and transient. 
 
  To cast away stones; either to mar a field by casting abroad stones upon it,  II Kings 3:19 II Kings 3:25 , or to cast away stones in demolishing a building. 
 
  To gather stones together; the opposite work. 
 
Since it is God's plan that men should be subjected to constant changes in this world, and should have no permanent and sure possession of earthly good, we ought to bear with cheerful resignation the vicissitudes of life, while we look to the future world for "a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God."

title: Ecclesiastes 3:11
text: Also he hath set the world in their heart; words of difficult interpretation.  A preferable rendering would be: "Also he hath set the world in their heart, because that no man can find out," etc.  The meaning would then be that God, understanding the inability of men to attain, by philosophic inquiry, to a full comprehension of his works and ways, has wisely set the world in their heart; that is, has occupied them to a large extent with its cares and labors, as a discipline that is good in its place and for the ends of probation. Their wisdom and happiness lie, then, not in vain endeavors to comprehend what is incomprehensible, but rather in submitting themselves in faith and patience to the appointments of their heavenly Father.  Our version gives the same idea in the form of a result instead of a reason: "He hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out," etc.

title: Ecclesiastes 3:14
text:
Whatsoever God doeth; in ordering the course of human affairs.  His arrangements are unchangeable, and above human control. 
 
  Should fear before him; in view of his supremacy over them.

title: Ecclesiastes 3:15
text: Requireth that which is past; looks it up, as it were, for the purpose of causing it to exist again.  This includes both the natural succession of creatures, fruits, and seasons, and the general course of human events.

title: Ecclesiastes 3:17
text:
There; at God's tribunal. 
 
  For every purpose and for every work; that is, for bringing them into judgment.

title: Ecclesiastes 3:18
text: Concerning the estate of the sons of men; or, It is in behalf of the sons of men; namely, that God deals with them as stated in  Ecclesiastes 3:16 .

title: Ecclesiastes 3:19
text:
vv 19-21. 
 
  That which befalleth--turn to dust again; the simple meaning of these words is, that men and bests alike suffer bodily death.  Psalms 49:20   The "one thing" that befalls both, is the death of the body; the "one breath" of both, is the breath of animal life; the "one place" to which both go is the dust. 
 
  Who knoweth; who can discern by his outward senses?  At death the spirit of a man goes upward to God who gave it,  Ecclesiastes 12:7 , while the spirit of a beast goes downward to the earth.  But this is something beyond the sphere of human observation.  So far as this world is concerned, "as the one dieth so dieth the other." 
 
Sin has brought death upon our bodies and placed them on a level with the bodies of beasts.  But from this deep humiliation Christ will deliver all his people, for he will raise them up at the last day, and present them before his Father's throne, made perfect in soul and body, with everlasting joy.

title: Ecclesiastes 3:22
text:
To see what shall be after him; in the future of this world.  Since no man can foresee what shall be after him, he should with a cheerful spirit enjoy the present gifts of God's providence.  The Preacher does not mean a dissolute enjoyment of this world, without the fear of God, but an enjoyment which is in his fear.   Ecclesiastes 11:9 Ecclesiastes 12:13  
 
We can know no more of the future than what God has been pleased to reveal in his word.  While then we faithfully perform the duties of the present hour, we can safely leave in his hands all that awaits us here and hereafter.

title: Ecclesiastes 4:1
text: Returned, and considered; considered again; took a second view.

title: Ecclesiastes 4:2
text:
vv 2-3. 
 
  Wherefore I praised the dead--done under the sun; the Preacher is looking at this life simply as a scene of vanity and oppression, without reference to its connection with the life to come.  Thus regarded, it seems to his earnest spirit an evil and not a good, so that the best thing is to have no experience of it.

title: Ecclesiastes 4:4
text:
Right work; skilful and successful undertaking. 
 
  Is envied of his neighbor; this is the trouble connected with successful activity. 
 
Although industry is better than idleness, yet we ought not to set our heart upon present enjoyment from the successful accomplishment of our worldly enterprises; for prosperity brings in its train envy, opposition, and many other annoyances.

title: Ecclesiastes 4:5
text: Eateth his own flesh; wastes his estate, without renewing it by industry: one of the troubles of indolence.

title: Ecclesiastes 4:6
text: Both the hands full with travail; these words imply, that the increase of one's estate is usually the increase of his trouble.

title: Ecclesiastes 4:7
text: I returned, and I saw vanity; I considered another example of vanity, that of the miser who toils for wealth without an heir.

title: Ecclesiastes 4:9
text:
vv 9-12. 
 
  Two are better than one--a threefold cord is not quickly broken; examples to show the advantages of union in human affairs. 
 
  They have a good reward for their labor; because by union they are able to accomplish it successfully. 
 
In all human labors union is a chief source of strength and comfort.

title: Ecclesiastes 4:14
text: He cometh; the poor and wise child.  His wisdom elevates him from a prison to the throne of the old king.

title: Ecclesiastes 4:15
text:
The living which walk; walk with the king as his subjects. 
 
  With the second child; with the wise child already named, who is called second, because he reigns next after the old king, in his stead.

title: Ecclesiastes 4:16
text:
That have been before them; before these two kings as their subjects. 
 
  Shall not rejoice in him; because death has removed him from the throne; or because the next generation shall be alienated from him, so that to himself the final issue of his wisdom shall be trouble. 
 
It is the high prerogative of wisdom to raise men from obscurity to eminent stations.  Yet their greatness cannot continue by reason of death, and besides, it generally brings to them more personal trouble than comfort; so that they, in common with all other men, must place their final hope in the rest that remaineth for the people of God.

title: Ecclesiastes 5:1
text:
Keep thy foot; this and the six following verses contain a warning against inconsiderateness in God's service, in respect to sacrifices, prayers, and vows. 
 
  To hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools; compare  I Samuel 15:22  
 
An obedient and teachable spirit is more acceptable to God than all outward services, which are often performed in an inconsiderate and presumptuous way.

title: Ecclesiastes 5:2
text:
To utter any thing; in prayer.  The thought of his majesty should make our words few and well pondered.   Matthew 6:7-8  
 
Many a prayer which men call eloquent is abominable in God's sight, because it comes from a spirit of levity and self-complacency.  True reverence for him will check the vain flow of words.

title: Ecclesiastes 5:3
text: A dream cometh--and a fool's voice is known; that is, As a dream cometh, so a fool's voice is known.  A fool's words poured out at random are like the confused images of a troubled dream.

title: Ecclesiastes 5:6
text:
Cause thy flesh to sin; bring guilt and trouble upon thee by a hasty vow that will not be fulfilled. 
 
  Before the angel; the word angel means messenger.  Here we are probably to understand the priest, as appointed by God to expound to men the Levitical law. 
 
  It was an error; the matter of vowing.  By saying this, he attempts to excuse himself from paying it. 
 
God will not allow men to mock him by vain promises.  For this reason hasty vows are to be discouraged, lest they who make them should repent of them, and neglect their fulfilment, and thus bring guilt upon their souls.

title: Ecclesiastes 5:8
text: There be higher than they; the reference is plainly to God's tribunal.   Ecclesiastes 12:14   If there were no judgment to come, we might well wonder at the violence and oppression with which the earth is filled.  The only adequate explanation is that which the Preacher himself gives at the close of the book: "God shall bring every work into judgment."

title: Ecclesiastes 5:10
text:
vv10-12. 
 
  Shall not be satisfied with silver--they are increased that eat them--will not suffer him to sleep; three of the vanities of wealth: it does not satisfy; it brings an increase of retinue and expenditure; it deprives its owners of sleep.

title: Ecclesiastes 5:13
text:
There is a sore evil--wrath with his sickness; a fourth double vanity of wealth: after a life of toil and care in accumulating it, it is liable to be all lost to both the owner and his heirs, and must at all events be left behind at death. 
 
  To their hurt; go their final sorrow and vexation by the loss of them. 
 
  Evil travail; misfortune. 
 
  Naked shall he return; the loss of wealth by "evil travail" leads the Preacher's thoughts to its final and inevitable loss at death.

title: Ecclesiastes 5:18
text:
It is good and comely for one to eat and to drink; in view of the vanity of wealth, the Preacher again recommends the contented and cheerful enjoyment of God's present gifts. 
 
Since riches are unsatisfying, uncertain, attended with an increase of trouble and anxiety, and must all be left behind at death, the wise man will be contented with the supply of his daily wants, and will lay up his treasure in heaven.

title: Ecclesiastes 5:20
text:
The days of his life; the evils that attend them. 
 
  Answereth him in the joy of his heart; answers his desire in the joy with which he fills his heart.  The thankful and contented enjoyment of God's present gifts causes him to forget the ills with which life is checkered.

title: Ecclesiastes 6:1
text:
There is an evil; the Preacher has shown that the power to enjoy good aright is the gift of God, and is the sum of earthly blessings.  Ecclesiastes 5:18-20   He now considers the opposite case. 
 
It is easy for God to imbitter to men all their earthly possessions, so that while they are surrounded by wealth their souls shall be in the deepest poverty.  The true enjoyment of life lies not in the abundance of outward good, but rather in a cheerful and contented spirit; especially in a humble resignation of ourselves to his all-powerful disposal, with unwavering faith in him for the present and the future.

title: Ecclesiastes 6:2
text:
Giveth him not power to eat thereof; either through the influence of tormenting passions, as avarice and envy; or through sickness and other calamities. 
 
  A stranger; another than himself.

title: Ecclesiastes 6:3
text: Be not filled with good--have no burial; live without enjoying life, and come to a disgraceful end.

title: Ecclesiastes 6:4
text: Name shall be covered with darkness; none shall hear of it.

title: Ecclesiastes 6:5
text: This; the untimely birth.  For the thought, compare  Ecclesiastes 4:3 .

title: Ecclesiastes 6:6
text: Do not all go to one place? that is, since in his long life he has seen no good, what is the profit of living long, as in the end the aged must with all others go to the grave?

title: Ecclesiastes 6:7
text:
For his mouth; to satisfy his bodily wants. 
 
  Is not filled; is ever craving more.

title: Ecclesiastes 6:8
text:
What hath the wise more than the fool? that is, in respect to what has just been named.  In their bodily wants, wise men and fools stand on a level. 
 
  The poor; the poor wise man. 
 
  Knoweth to walk; to walk wisely.

title: Ecclesiastes 6:9
text:
The sight of the eyes; the sight and enjoyment of present good. 
 
  The wandering of the desire; after absent good.

title: Ecclesiastes 6:10
text:
That which hath been is named already; or, that which is hath been named already.  Compare  Ecclesiastes 1:9 Ecclesiastes 3:15 . 
 
  Known; from all past experience. 
 
  That it is man: neither may he contend with him that is mightier than he; that is, weak, frail, and perishing man, who occupies this world subject to the sovereign appointment of God, and unable to change the course of human affairs which He has established.

title: Ecclesiastes 6:11
text: What is man the better? literally, "What profit is there to man?" that is, what satisfying good has he?

title: Ecclesiastes 6:12
text: In this life--what shall be after him; two reasons are given why there is no profit to man: first, no one can show any satisfying good; secondly, no one can understand the future.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:2
text:
That is the end of all man; that is, the end of all men is seen in the house of mourning. 
 
  Will lay it to his heart; will meditate there on the vanity of life, and be thus led to prepare himself for death. 
 
God is continually opening to the living the house of mourning, that they may enter and consider what awaits them.  The heart of the wise willingly dwells there.  It is only the foolish who seek by noisy mirth to exclude from their minds all thoughts of death and judgment to come.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:5
text: The rebuke of the wise; another painful thing which is better than mirth and flattery.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:6
text:
The crackling of thorns; their flame is noisy and fierce, but soon over. 
 
The enjoyment of those who make earthly pleasure their chief good is turbulent and short-lived, and ends in darkness and sorrow.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:7
text:
Oppression; suffered. 
 
  Maketh a wise man mad; it tends to this result.  The verse notices two opposite temptations to which the wise are exposed in this world of vanity and crookedness.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:8
text:
The end of a thing; its successful accomplishment, which requires patience and perseverance.  We must wait till an undertaking is through, before we can speak confidently of it. 
 
  The patient in spirit--the proud in spirit; the proud are properly contrasted with the patient, since pride is the root of anger. 
 
We should not be too much elated with the prosperous beginning of an enterprise, but rather wait to see the final issue; since many a work commenced with gladness ends in sorrow, while "they that sow in tears shall reap in joy."

title: Ecclesiastes 7:10
text: What is the cause; the Preacher forbids a complaining spirit, which is always contrasting the evils of the present with the good of the past.  This is a work of impatience and folly.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:11
text: Wisdom is good with an inheritance; or, "as good as an inheritance," seems to contain the true idea, which the following verse confirms.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:13
text:
Consider the work of God; his sovereign ordering of human affairs. 
 
  That which he hath made crooked; see  Ecclesiastes 1:15 . 
 
To fret ourselves on account of those evils which God has made irremediable, is both foolish and wicked.  The should be quietly borne, as a part of the discipline which he has laid upon us as sinners, for our spiritual good.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:14
text: Find nothing after him; find out nothing that shall be after him. God has so mingled prosperity and adversity, that no man can find out what awaits him in the future of this life.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:15
text:
Perisheth in his righteousness; for righteousness' sake. 
 
  Prolongeth his life in his wickedness; through his wickedness.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:16
text:
vv 16-17. 
 
  Be not righteous overmuch, neither make thyself overwise--be not overmuch wicked; be cautious against a false righteousness, on the one hand, which is corrupted by pride and self-conceit; and on the other, against the out-breakings of wickedness and folly, since both lead to destruction.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:18
text:
Take hold of this; namely, my counsel. 
 
  Withdraw not thy hand; do not let it go; the opposite of taking hold upon it. 
 
  Come forth of them all; of the dangers above referred to.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:20
text: For there is not a just man--and sinneth not; he has just said,  Ecclesiastes 7:19 , "Wisdom strengtheneth the wise."  He now shows why such strengthening is needed.  It is because, in a world of universal frailty and sinfulness, wisdom alone guides us aright.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:21
text:
vv 21-22. 
 
  All words that are spoken; words of reproach uttered against thyself.  Trouble not thyself about finding them out, since thou art in the like condemnation with respect to others. 
 
We should never go in search of uncharitable rumors concerning ourselves, but rather pass them by unheeded, remembering how often we have spoken uncharitably of others.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:23
text: All this; what the Preacher has recorded of his search after good. he found out that "all is vanity;" but wisdom itself, that is, a comprehension of God's works and ways, remained far from him.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:24
text: Far off-- exceeding deep; as are the works and ways of God. Compare  Ecclesiastes 3:11 Ecclesiastes 8:17 .

title: Ecclesiastes 7:27
text: Counting one by one; adding the result of one trial to that of another.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:28
text:
A woman; a woman of true wisdom. 
 
  Among all those; among all this number, that is, among a thousand. The reference seems to be to Solomon's experience of the women who belonged to his royal establishment.  Among such a thousand, selected for their personal charms, and many of them from among the heathen nations, nourished in idleness and luxury, and intriguing with each other for the monarch's favor, no better result could have been expected.  Here was not the place to find Ruths and Hannahs.

title: Ecclesiastes 7:29
text: All that is excellent in man is from God; his sinfulness and folly are his own.

title: Ecclesiastes 8:1
text:
Who knoweth the interpretation of a thing? that is, as the wise man. 
 
  The boldness of his face shall be changed; his bold air shall be changed to the serenity and dignity of wisdom.  Some render this clause thus: "The strength of his countenance," that is, his firm and assured look, "shall be doubled."

title: Ecclesiastes 8:2
text: Obedience to the civil magistrate is a matter not of human expediency, but of divine authority.  We are released from it only when he requires what God forbids.

title: Ecclesiastes 8:3
text:
Be not hasty to go out of his sight; do not hastily withdraw thyself from his service.   Ecclesiastes 10:4   To stand before a king, is to serve him,  I Kings 12:6 ; hence, to leave his presence, is to quit his service. 
 
  Stand not; be not engaged. 
 
  He doeth whatsoever pleaseth him; and will therefore punish all evil deeds.

title: Ecclesiastes 8:5
text:
Feel no evil thing; or, "know no evil thing;" that is, will not suffer for disobedience.   Ecclesiastes 8:3  
 
  Time and judgment; the right time and way of doing a thing.

title: Ecclesiastes 8:6
text: Because to every purpose--great upon him; more literally thus: "For to every puropse there is time and judgment; for the evil of man is great upon him;" that is, time and judgment are necessary to every purpose, because of the evil and uncertainty which belong to human life, and make every good undertaking difficult.

title: Ecclesiastes 8:7
text: Since it is the plan of God's providence that we should be ignorant of the future, and subject to disappointment in all our undertakings, we ought to unite, with the wise selection of times and means, a spirit of humble dependence upon him and patient submission to his sovereign will.

title: Ecclesiastes 8:8
text:
Deliver those that are given to it; namely, from death. 
 
The great and the small are alike helpless in the day of death; and ought therefore to be alike humble and diligent in preparing to meet God.

title: Ecclesiastes 8:10
text:
And so I saw the wicked buried; the wicked who had been in power,  Ecclesiastes 8:9 , and trusted in their wickedness,  Ecclesiastes 8:8 , the Preacher sees buried and forgotten. 
 
  From the place of the holy; probably from Jerusalem, the place of those consecrated to God's service. 
 
  So done,; had been given to wickedness,  Ecclesiastes 8:8 , and ruled over men to their own harm,  Ecclesiastes 8:9 .

title: Ecclesiastes 8:11
text:
Is not executed speedily; in noticing the final end of the wicked, the Preacher also notices the delay of God's judgment, and its abuse by men. 
 
Nowhere does the desperate wickedness of men show itself more clearly, than in the encouragement which they take from God's gracious forbearance, to harden themselves in iniquity.  Thus they turn to their deeper damnation what he gave them for their salvation.

title: Ecclesiastes 8:14
text: There is a vanity; though it will in the end be well with the righteous and ill with the wicked, yet, in respect to the course of events in this world, "there is one event to the righteous, and to the wicked."   Ecclesiastes 9:2   Both are alike subject to "the sufferings of this present time," and to death itself.  The only possible reconciliation of this verse with the two preceding, is the doctrine of a judgment to come.  This the preacher asserts at the close of the book.

title: Ecclesiastes 8:15
text: Then I commended mirth; see  Ecclesiastes 2:24 Ecclesiastes 3:22 .

title: Ecclesiastes 8:17
text:
Cannot find out the work; see the vanity of earthly wisdom is shown from the impossibility of its accomplishing what it undertakes, namely, to comprehend God's ways and works.  See  Ecclesiastes 7:23 . 
 
Since God's judgments are unsearchable, and his ways past finding out, true wisdom lies not in endeavoring to comprehend that which is incomprehensible, but in the cheerful resignation of ourselves to his will with a believing, loving, and obedient spirit.

title: Ecclesiastes 9:1
text:
Are in the hand of God; at the close of the preceding chapter it is said, "No man can find out the work that is done under the sun."  The reason is now given: All is controlled by God, whose ways are unsearchable. 
 
  Knoweth either love or hatred by all that is before them; or more literally thus: "No man knoweth either love or hatred: all is before them."  He cannot tell, from mere outward things, whether love or hatred is to be his lot: all is in the unknown future. 
 
Our highest wisdom lies in conforming to the plan of God's providence, and making his will the law of our being.  As the righteous and the wicked are alike subject to suffering, misfortune, and death, we should not set our hearts on the uninterrupted enjoyment of earthly good; but cheerfully enjoy God's present gifts, while we hold ourselves ready to part with them at his bidding.  The result of all our labors is at his disposal, and we ought to unite, with the diligent use of means, a spirit resigned to his will and prepared for disappointment.  In this world, labor for the good of others, however well-directed, is not always appreciated, and we ought not to expect from our fellow men too much or our services.  We must soon be done with time, and it becomes us to do the work which God puts into our hands with our might, and lay up for ourselves a treasure in heaven.

title: Ecclesiastes 9:2
text: Sweareth; that is, profanely.

title: Ecclesiastes 9:3
text: They go to the dead; where there is no more hope.   Ecclesiastes 9:4

title: Ecclesiastes 9:4
text:
vv 4-6. 
 
  Reward; enjoyment of their earthly toil. 
 
  Neither have they any more a portion; these words contain the clue to the Preacher's meaning: The dead have done with earth and all its concerns; they lie in the grave unconscious and forgotten.  He confines what he here says to the present life, not following the soul to the world of spirits.  Compare our Saviour's words,  John 9:4 .

title: Ecclesiastes 9:7
text:
vv 7-10. 
 
  Now accepteth thy works; smiles upon thee, and gives thee the enjoyment of them.  This implies that they are done in his fear.  In view of the truth that "the dead have no portion" in this life, the living are exhorted to a cheerful enjoyment of God's gifts and diligence in God's service.

title: Ecclesiastes 9:11
text: Returned, and saw; took another view of God's sovereignty over men and their works.

title: Ecclesiastes 9:16
text: The poor man's wisdom is despised; his past manifestation of wisdom does not secure present regard to his counsels.

title: Ecclesiastes 9:17
text:
In quiet; in the quiet counsels of the wise.  "Wisdom is justified of her children."   Matthew 11:19  
 
  More than the cry--among fools; the counsels of wisdom are more regarded, and produce more salutary results.  Yet a foolish multitude will follow the boisterous cry of a foolish leader, and despise the counsels of the poor wise man.

title: Ecclesiastes 9:18
text: One sinner destroyeth; by his folly, the effects of which are here opposed to those of wisdom.

title: Ecclesiastes 10:1
text: The higher a man's standing and reputation, the more injurious to himself and others is the exhibition of folly.  A little foolishness may overshadow great wisdom.

title: Ecclesiastes 10:2
text: At his right hand; he uses it skilfully.

title: Ecclesiastes 10:3
text:
Walketh by the way; appears in public. 
 
  Saith to every one; by his actions. 
 
When folly appears in public it always betrays itself.

title: Ecclesiastes 10:5
text: As an error which proceedeth; that is, an error such as proceedeth. The error consists in exalting the mean and unworthy to office, a common evil in the despotic governments of the East.

title: Ecclesiastes 10:6
text:
The rich; the same as "princes" in the following verse, who unite wealth with nobleness and intelligence. 
 
The elevation of unworthy men to offices of power and trust is a heavy calamity to the people.  Whether it proceed from their rulers, or, as in the case of free governments, from themselves, the result will be corruption, misrule, and misery.

title: Ecclesiastes 10:8
text:
vv 8-10. 
 
  He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it--wisdom is profitable to direct; general meaning: the dangers and difficulties of life are many; but wisdom is profitable to direct in them all.

title: Ecclesiastes 10:12
text: Gracious; acceptable and useful.

title: Ecclesiastes 10:14
text: It is often the case, that the less men have to say that will benefit themselves or others, the more they abound in words.  "A wise head makes a short tongue," is the true Arabic proverb.

title: Ecclesiastes 10:15
text: How to go to the city; a particular instance of his ignorance, which stands to represent all other cases.  As much as to say, when he undertakes the simplest enterprise, he knows not how and where to find the means of success.

title: Ecclesiastes 10:16
text: The primary qualification for ruling others is ability to rule ourselves.  They who destroy themselves by self-indulgence, will destroy also the people committed to their care.

title: Ecclesiastes 10:18
text: The house droppeth through; lets water drop through the roof. Here, again, we have a particular case to illustrate a general principle.

title: Ecclesiastes 10:20
text: Vain is the hope of escaping punishment by the secrecy of our evil deeds.  God is able, in numberless unforeseen ways to bring them to light here, and he will expose them all hereafter in the presence of men and angels.

title: Ecclesiastes 11:1
text:
Cast thy bread upon the waters; either bread given in alms, or seed-corn, in allusion to the practice of sowing upon land that has been overflowed.  Labor and give cheerfully without any present prospect of reward, knowing that in due time the gracious recompense will come. 
 
The best provision that we can make for the future is, not to hoard up our property and withhold it from the needy, but to give liberally to all; for "he that hath pity upon the poor, lendeth unto the Lord; and that which he hath given will he pay him again."

title: Ecclesiastes 11:2
text:
To seven, and also to eight; to all who need thy charity.  See  Proverbs 6:16 . 
 
  What evil shall be; evil that shall make the charity of others needful for thee.  Compare  Proverbs 21:13 . 
 
The uncertainty hanging over the future, which some men give as a reason for getting and holding all they can, is truly a reason for bestowing freely.

title: Ecclesiastes 11:3
text: If the clouds be full--where the tree falleth; in nature, and in the course of human history, there are fixed tendencies which the wise will regard.

title: Ecclesiastes 11:4
text:
vv 4,6. 
 
We should keep diligently at work in God's service, disregarding present inconveniences and unfavorable appearances.  The duty is ours; the reward God will give when and in what measure he pleases.

title: Ecclesiastes 11:5
text:
The way of the spirit; the mode of its union with the body.  Some render, "the way of the wind."  Compare  John 3:8 .  In Hebrew, "wind" and "spirit" are expressed by the same word. 
 
When we meet with so many mysteries in nature, we should not be offended with mysteries in God's providence and the work of redemption.

title: Ecclesiastes 11:7
text: The light is sweet; light and seeing the sun are here emblems of life.

title: Ecclesiastes 11:9
text:
Rejoice, O young man--God will bring thee into judgment; let thy pursuit of happiness and all thy youthful enjoyments be in the fear of God, and with a constant remembrance of the account thou must give of them at his tribunal.  Compare  Ecclesiastes 9:7-9 . 
 
A deep sense of God's presence, and habitual reverence for his authority, are the great security to the young against the pursuit of sinful pleasure.  They who fear God, and make him their portion, will enjoy all that this world is capable of giving, and be prepared for the higher enjoyments of eternity.

title: Ecclesiastes 12:1
text:
vv 1-6. 
 
These verses continue the admonition to the young begun in the preceding chapter, and add a figurative description of the sorrows of old age. 
 
  Be not darkened, nor the clouds return after the rain; old age is represented as a season of clouds and rain, in which the light of the heavenly bodies is darkened. 
 
  Keepers of the house--strong men; the human body is compared to a mansion, of which the limbs are the keepers. 
 
  The grinders cease; the teeth, compared to the women who daily grind at the mill in all eastern countries. 
 
  Those that look out of the windows; the eyes, represented as females looking out at the windows. 
 
  The doors shall be shut--the sound of the grinding is low; as the sound of the grinding gradually sinks into silence, the doors also that lead into the street are shut; that is, old age is inactive and keeps at home. 
 
  Rise up at the voice of the bird; early rise up in his couch; the slightest sound shall break his slumbers. 
 
  Daughters of music; singing women, who represent here the organs of speech and hearing. 
 
  Afraid of that which is high--fears shall be in the way; on account of their feebleness and liability to fall. 
 
  The almond-tree; generally understood as an emblem of grey hairs. 
 
  The grasshopper; alighting on them; that is, the smallest weight.  Leviticus 11:22  
 
  Desire; the animal appetites. 
 
  Or ever; before. 
 
  Silver cord--golden bowl; of the hall lamp, as an emblem of life; or the allusion may be to the cord and bucket used in drawing water. 
 
  The pitcher--the wheel; the means of drawing and carrying water: the drawing of water represents the activity of life. 
 
They who devote to God's service the vigorous and joyful days of youth, will not be forsaken by him when they are old and grey-headed; but they who forget God in their youthful prime, and give it themselves up to sinful pleasures, must, if not cut off prematurely in their transgressions, come to a comfortless old age, and, continuing as they have lived, must die under God's wrath and curse.

title: Ecclesiastes 12:7
text: To God who gave it; it returns to its Creator, that its deeds done in the body may be brought into judgment.   Ecclesiastes 12:14   Thus the Preacher teaches the conscious existence of the spirit after death, as a subject of rewards and penalties.

title: Ecclesiastes 12:11
text:
Goads; stimulating to right action. 
 
  Nails fastened; they make a deep impression upon the memory and conscience, and serve for the regulation of life.  Compare  Isaiah 22:23-24 . 
 
  Masters of assemblies; teachers of the people. 
 
  Which are given; namely, the words of the wise. 
 
  From one shepherd; from God, the one great Shepherd.

title: Ecclesiastes 12:13
text:
The conclusion; the final result to which the Preacher's observation and experience have brought him. 
 
The way of happiness here and salvation hereafter is exceedingly plain and simple.  It consists in fearing God and keeping his commandments, the chief of which is, that we believe on Jesus Christ his Son.

title: Ecclesiastes 12:14
text:
Every work--every secret thing; since no such judgment takes place in the present life, it must be that which awaits men when "the spirit shall return unto God who gave it."  All parts of the book must be interpreted in harmony with this its final declaration. 
 
Since God shall bring every secret thing into judgment, vain are all attempts to hide our sins from ourselves, or from our fellow men.  To those who repent and believe in Christ, his blood will be a covering, and this covering we all need. 
 
In this book the Spirit of inspiration was manifestly preparing the church for the fuller revelations of the gospel.  God's promise to Abraham, and in him to all his seed, was, "I am thy exceeding great reward."  This promise cannot, as the Preacher shows, be fulfilled in God's earthly gifts.  Its fulfilment must be reserved for the world to come.

title: Song of Solomon 1:2
text: Let him kiss me; the spouse speaks of the king.

title: Song of Solomon 1:3
text:
vv 3-4. 
 
  The virgins; the bride's "companions that follow her."  Psalms 45:14   These are brought in with her into the king's palace. The bride is the church in her unity; the retinue of honorable virgins that follow her, seems to represent the multiplicity of her members. 
 
God has given to Jesus "a name which is above every name."  To all who have had a true discovery of their own emptiness and his infinite fulness, it is "as ointment poured forth:" and it draws them to Christ in sweet confidence and love.

title: Song of Solomon 1:5
text:
Black; scorched by the sun.   Song of Solomon 1:6   Blackness is an emblem of adversity and persecution.   Job 30:30 Lamentations 4:8  
 
  Daughters of Jerusalem; these are in reality the same as the virgins that follow the bride, but under another figure; Jerusalem representing the church as a mother, and the "daughters of Jerusalem" as her members. 
 
  As the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon; that is, black, like the tents of Kedar, which were made of black goat's hair; but comely, as the curtains of Solomon.  Kedar was an Arabian tribe. 
 
"The bride, the Lamb's wife," is comely in the eyes of God, even in her deepest humiliation.  Though others may despise her, he will still honor her and have mercy upon her.

title: Song of Solomon 1:6
text:
Look not upon me; with amazement and abhorrence. 
 
  The sun hath looked upon me; hath scorched me.   Isaiah 49:10  
 
  My mother's children; Edom, Moab, and Ammon, who here represent all the gentile nations.  These were the brethren of the Israelites by descent, and so sprung from the bride's mother. See note on  Song of Solomon 3:4 . 
 
  The vineyards; of her brethren.  She has been in servitude to the Gentiles as a punishment for her sins. 
 
The strength of the church lies in her union with Christ.  When she forsakes him, he leaves her for a season to the oppression of the wicked, without any power to deliver herself.

title: Song of Solomon 1:7
text:
O thou whom my soul loveth; the bride to the king, in her separation from him. 
 
  One that turneth aside; or, one that is veiled.  The veil is a sign of mourning and depression. 
 
  Thy companions; the friends of the bridegroom, who are, spiritually considered, not different from the companions of the bride, being all who love Christ.

title: Song of Solomon 1:8
text:
Go thy way forth; the chief Shepherd walks among the under-shepherds.  If the spouse would find him, she must seek him in the discharge of her duty, where he is to be found. 
 
If we would find God, we must seek him in the ways of his appointment.

title: Song of Solomon 1:9
text:
I have compared thee; the spouse has now found the king.  What follows, to the end of  Song of Solomon 2:7 , is a mutual discourse between the two.  She calls him her "beloved," and he addresses her as his "love." This distinction is observed throughout the book. 
 
  To a company of horses; she is compared to the cavalry of Egypt, on account of her invincible might.  Compare  Song of Solomon 6:10 . 
 
vv 9-17. 
 
The graces with which Christ has invested his people he regards with delight; and they rest with unspeakable satisfaction in his infinite uncreated excellence.  Hence springs a blessed communion between the Redeemer and his redeemed.

title: Song of Solomon 1:10
text:
vv 10-11. 
 
  Rows--chains--studs; the bride's ornaments are her spiritual graces.   Psalms 45:13-14 Revelation of John 19:8

title: Song of Solomon 1:12
text: Sitteth at his table; to sup with his bride, a symbol of spiritual communion.   Song of Solomon 5:1 Isaiah 25:6 Revelation of John 3:20

title: Song of Solomon 1:14
text:
Camphire; a shrub with large clusters of fragrant whitish flowers, very grateful to oriental women. 
 
  Engedi; a fountain on the western shore of the Dead sea, where were gardens in ancient times.   I Samuel 24:1

title: Song of Solomon 1:17
text: Cedar--fir; the costliness of the palace which the king has provided for his spouse, represents her glory and excellence.

title: Song of Solomon 2:1
text: Rose of Sharon--lily; emblems of loveliness.

title: Song of Solomon 2:3
text: The apple-tree among the trees of the wood; the apple-tree is commended for its precious fruit, in contrast with the barren forest-trees.  It probably includes the citron, and other trees with fragrant fruits.

title: Song of Solomon 2:4
text: His banner over me; the church is compared to an army, and the love of Christ is the banner under which she marches. Compare  Song of Solomon 6:10 .

title: Song of Solomon 2:5
text:
Sick of love; overpowered with the longing desires of love.  For the spiritual meaning, compare  Psalms 42:1-2 Psalms 63:1-11 . 
 
He who has once tasted the sweetness of God's love in Christ, can be satisfied with nothing short of its continued manifestation.  In its absence, his soul "longeth, yea, even fainteth" for its renewal; and his heart and flesh "crieth out for the living God."

title: Song of Solomon 2:7
text:
By the roes, and by the hinds; by all that is lovely. 
 
  Till he please; or, according to the Hebrew text, "till she please," as in the early English versions.  It will then be the bridegroom's charge that his love, the church, be undisturbed.  These words, which occur twice afterwards, always form the close of a scene. 
 
The welfare of Zion is as the holiness of her individual members.  The Saviour tenderly adjures all who love him and his church, not to do any thing which shall hinder her union and communion with himself, wherein lie her strength, comfort, and usefulness.

title: Song of Solomon 2:8
text:
The voice of my beloved; a new scene opens.  The bride, in her winter retreat, hears the voice of her beloved coming in exultation to call her forth.  Winter, like the scorching of the sun, is a symbol of adversity and depression; and spring, of returning prosperity. 
 
After the winter of adversity, God always appears for the relief of his people.

title: Song of Solomon 2:9
text:
Behind our wall; behind the wall of the house where the bride and her companions are.  Christ comes to comfort his church. 
 
  Looketh forth; rather, "looketh in."  He calls to his bride from without.

title: Song of Solomon 2:11
text:
vv 11-13. 
 
Christ's presence with his church fills her with the voice of gladness and singing, and makes every thing within her borders green and fruitful.

title: Song of Solomon 2:14
text:
Secret places; crevices, or holes, where she hides. 
 
  Stairs; shelving rocks, which are climbed like stairs.  He compares his bride, in her retreat, to a dove that has taken refuge in the clefts of the rocks.   Jeremiah 48:28

title: Song of Solomon 2:15
text:
Take us the foxes; the bride has listened to the call of the bridegroom, and come forth to active service.  She now visits with him their common vineyard.   Song of Solomon 7:12   This must be cleared of every thing that can injure it.  In other words, all hindrances to the fruitfulness of Zion must be removed. 
 
If God's people would enjoy his presence and blessing, they must put away every iniquity and stumbling-block.

title: Song of Solomon 2:16
text: Feedeth among the lilies; delights himself with the graces of his bride.

title: Song of Solomon 2:17
text:
Until the day break; literally, "breathe."   Song of Solomon 4:6 .  This should, according to many, be understood of the cool evening breeze.  Genesis 3:8  
 
  Shadows flee away; disappear at sunset.   Psalms 102:11 Psalms 109:23  
 
  Turn, my beloved; return to the mountains whence thou camest.  Song of Solomon 2:8   She consents to his departure till the evening.

title: Song of Solomon 3:1
text: I sought him, but I found him not; the first five verses of this chapter describe the bride's longing desire after her beloved in his absence, and her unsuccessful search for him.   Jeremiah 29:12-14

title: Song of Solomon 3:4
text:
Her that conceived me; spiritually interpreted, the bride's mother is not essentially different from the bride herself.  The one is the church viewed spiritually, in her power to produce and perpetuate a holy seed, and the other, the church viewed as that seed. 
 
Christ will be found of all who earnestly seek him in the ways of his appointment.

title: Song of Solomon 3:5
text: Till he please; see note to  Song of Solomon 2:7 .

title: Song of Solomon 3:6
text:
Who is this; a new picture.  The bride comes out of the wilderness to meet the heavenly Bridegroom, gloriously arrayed in wedding attire and fragrant with perfumes. 
 
  The wilderness; into which she has been banished.  This is a symbol of persecution and distress,  Revelation of John 12:6 Revelation of John 12:14 ; the same as the winter season,  Song of Solomon 2:11 . 
 
  Like pillars of smoke; surrounded with clouds of fragrant incense. Her graces are a sweet savor to God. 
 
The church never appears so glorious as in her return to God by hearty repentance and faith, after the night of affliction and chastisement.

title: Song of Solomon 3:8
text:
Because of fear in the night; to guard against fear in the night. 
 
The church is safe in communion with her omnipotent Redeemer.  Zechariah 2:5 Zechariah 9:8

title: Song of Solomon 3:9
text: A chariot; this is for his bride and her companions, the daughters of Jerusalem.  Its precious materials represent the dignity and excellence of those who ride in it.

title: Song of Solomon 3:10
text: For the daughters of Jerusalem; more literally, "from the daughters of Jerusalem."  The midst of it is paved with their love for the King.

title: Song of Solomon 3:11
text:
His mother crowned him; the church is the mother of the heavenly Solomon, the greatest of all her sons, and also his bride.  Compare  Isaiah 62:5 .  In the same way the church, viewed in one aspect, is the bride's mother; in another, the bride herself.  See note on  Song of Solomon 3:4 .  The Bridegroom and bride are also brother and sister. This blending of figures in allegory is both natural and beautiful. 
 
In his espousals to the church, Christ appears in heavenly glory, the object of unbounded love and admiration to all who belong to the household of faith.

title: Song of Solomon 4:1
text:
In this chapter the heavenly Solomon sets forth the beauty and majesty of his bride. 
 
  As a flock of goats; the comparison respects the hair. 
 
  Gilead; a region east of the Jordan, celebrated for the excellence of its pasture-grounds.

title: Song of Solomon 4:2
text: Like a flock of sheep; in whiteness.  What follows is added to show their soundness and vigor.

title: Song of Solomon 4:4
text: Like the tower of David; for strength and majesty.

title: Song of Solomon 4:6
text: Until the day break; see note on  Song of Solomon 2:17 .  From the mountains of myrrh and the hill of frankincense he gathers perfumes for his love, that she may be "perfumed with myrrh and frankincense."   Song of Solomon 3:6

title: Song of Solomon 4:7
text: The heavenly bride, the Lamb's wife, is "the perfection of beauty, the joy of the whole earth."  She embraces in herself all the true excellence that is found among men.

title: Song of Solomon 4:8
text:
Here begins a new representation, in which, for the first time, the bride is addressed by the title of "spouse." 
 
  Come with me from Lebanon; these words seem to be spoken on the top of Lebanon, where Solomon, who represents the heavenly Bridegroom, has been showing his bride the glory of his kingdom.  He calls her to take a like survey of it from the top of Amana and Hermon.  Deuteronomy 34:1 Revelation of John 21:10   The ridge of Hermon lies east of Lebanon.  It was called Shenir by the Amorites.   Deuteronomy 3:9   Amana was probably a peak of the same range, from which the river of the same name flowed. 
 
  From the lions' dens; that is, from the tops of the mountains, that abound in lions' dens.  In showing his bride these goodly possessions, the king gives her a pledge that she shall share with him dominion over them.

title: Song of Solomon 4:12
text:
Inclosed--shut up--sealed; guarded from intrusion, and reserved for the king's enjoyment. For the spiritual meaning, compare  II Corinthians 11:2 . 
 
Christ will not share with others the affections of his people.  If they would have him dwell in their garden, its fruits must be consecrated to him alone.

title: Song of Solomon 4:15
text:
A fountain of gardens; lying among gardens and watering them. 
 
  Streams from Lebanon; cool and refreshing.   Jeremiah 18:14

title: Song of Solomon 4:16
text:
Awake, O north wind; the wind is a symbol of the quickening and life-giving power of the Holy Spirit.   Ezekiel 37:9-10  
 
  My garden; in  Song of Solomon 4:12 , the spouse was herself a garden, and its precious fruits her graces.  Here she has charge of a garden.  The meaning is the same. 
 
The fruitfulness of God's people depends upon the presence and life-giving power of the Holy Spirit, by whom alone they can be made meet for communion with their Redeemer.

title: Song of Solomon 5:1
text:
I am come into my garden; this is the King's answer to the invitation of his bride in the last verse of the preceding chapter, from which it should not have been separated. 
 
  Eat, O friends; the friends of the bridegroom.  See note on  Song of Solomon 1:7 . 
 
Christ is prompt to answer the invitations of his friends, when they are made in sincerity; and his communion with them is "sweeter than honey and the honeycomb."  It is a feast "of fat things, full of marrow of wines on the lees well refined."   Isaiah 25:6

title: Song of Solomon 5:2
text:
A new picture begins here.  The bride, for her sinful indolence, is forsaken of her beloved, and seeks him sorrowing. 
 
  I sleep, but my heart waketh; the sleep of God's people is never total, like that of the world.  Though the bride is asleep, yet her heart is awake to hear the call of her beloved. 
 
  Open to me; compare  Revelation of John 3:20 . 
 
  My head is filled with dew; he pleads what he has undergone for her sake.  The dews of Palestine are very heavy.

title: Song of Solomon 5:3
text:
I have put off my coat; the church sunk in carnal ease and security, is reluctant to open to the Saviour. 
 
Spiritual slothfulness has its foundation in the want of fervent love towards Christ, and is therefore exceedingly guilty and offensive in his sight.

title: Song of Solomon 5:4
text:
Put in his hand; an earnest token of his desire to enter.  In its spiritual application, it denotes all the ways in which Christ arouses his slumbering people. 
 
Christ is too faithful to leave his church slumbering in sinful inaction.  By mingled judgments and mercies, accompanying his word and Spirit, he will arouse her to a sense of her duty, and bring her to repentance.

title: Song of Solomon 5:5
text:
Dropped with myrrh; her penitence is a sweet savor to God. 
 
The fingers of penitent believers drop with sweet-smelling myrrh. Their tears and confessions of sin and works meet for repentance, are most precious in God's sight, and will in due time be rewarded with his returning presence and favor.

title: Song of Solomon 5:6
text:
Failed when he spake; spoke a reproving word in withdrawing. 
 
Those who have backslidden from God are often left for a season in darkness, that they thus may feel more deeply the evil of sin, seek Christ more earnestly, and set a higher value upon his love.

title: Song of Solomon 5:7
text: When for their sins the Redeemer withdraws his presence from his people, they are helpless, and exposed to injuries and insults from the world that lies in wickedness.

title: Song of Solomon 5:8
text: Nothing can compensate the true believer for the loss of Christ's comforting presence, and he will not rest till he has recovered it.

title: Song of Solomon 5:9
text: What is thy beloved; this question of the daughters of Zion gives the bride occasion to set forth the excellences of her beloved.

title: Song of Solomon 5:10
text:
vv 10.16. 
 
In our Redeemer all excellences meet; he is "the chiefest among ten thousand;" "yea, he is altogether lovely."

title: Song of Solomon 5:12
text:
By the rivers of waters; which doves love to frequent. 
 
  Washed with milk; this denotes the whiteness of their plumage.  The dove is an emblem of innocence, guilelessness, and purity.

title: Song of Solomon 6:2
text:
Is gone down into his garden; the spouse in union with her beloved is herself "a garden inclosed," full of the precious fruits of righteousness.   Song of Solomon 4:12   Or, she stands in the midst of her garden and calls her beloved to partake of its fruits.   Song of Solomon 4:16   But, in leaving her beloved, she has left the heavenly garden also, and there she must seek him again. 
 
Christ dwells in his garden amid the fruits of holiness; and they who seek him there shall find him.

title: Song of Solomon 6:3
text:
I am my beloved's; the separation is now ended, and in the following verses the bridegroom sets forth the excellences of his bride. 
 
Christ's love for his people remains strong even in their departure from him; and when they return to him with all their heart, he will graciously receive them, and restore them to their former union and communion with himself.

title: Song of Solomon 6:4
text:
Tirzah; a pleasant city, for a time the capital of the kingdom of Israel.   I Kings 14:17 I Kings 15:21 II Kings 15:14  
 
  Terrible as an army with banners; see note on  Song of Solomon 1:9 . 
 
vv 4-10. 
 
However men may despise Christ's church, she is most precious in his eyes, and he will make her, by the gifts of his Spirit, "fair as the moon, clear as the sun," and to all her enemies, "terrible as an army with banners."

title: Song of Solomon 6:8
text: Queens--concubines--virgins; here, as in  Psalms 45:1-13 , the queen is represented as preeminent above all her attendants.  In the spiritual application, the words mean, that "the bride, the Lamb's wife," is loved and honored by all her members.

title: Song of Solomon 6:11
text: I went down; this is probably the beginning of a new representation.  The bridegroom has gone down into his garden, as in  Song of Solomon 6:2 .  There he is seized with longing affection for his absent spouse, and calls upon her to return, that he may behold her beauty.

title: Song of Solomon 6:12
text: Like the chariots of Amminadib; or, "the chariots of my willing people."  In either case, the reference is to return, that he may behold her beauty.

title: Song of Solomon 6:13
text:
Return, O Shulamite; Shulamite seems to be a symbolic name of the bride, having a designed resemblance to that of Solomon, who represents the heavenly Bridegroom, in both form and meaning.  This is more manifest in the Hebrew, thus: 
 
  Shelomoh, Solomon, that is, the Peaceful,  I Chronicles 22:9 ; 
 
  Shulammith, Shulamite, that is, the Peaceful, or the Reconciled. 
 
  That we may look; the king and his friends.  Compare  Song of Solomon 5:1 . 
 
  What will ye see; the words of the spouse, expressing a sense of her unworthiness. 
 
  As it were the company of two armies; or, "As it were the dances of Mahanaim;" that is, the exulting bands of angels that met Jacob on his return from Padanaram.   Genesis 32:1-2 .  This is the response of the bridegroom.  Mahanaim means, two hosts. 
 
When the believer has the deepest sense of his unworthiness, he is most excellent and honorable in the sight of God.

title: Song of Solomon 7:1
text:
How beautiful; in the first part of this chapter the praises of the bride are repeated. 
 
  With shoes; compare  Ezekiel 16:10 .  These, like all her other ornaments, are the gift of her heavenly Bridegroom. 
 
  O prince's daughter; she is of royal lineage, a "king's daughter."  Psalms 45:13  This is a symbol of her dignity.

title: Song of Solomon 7:4
text:
Fish-pools; for clearness and purity. 
 
  Heshbon; a city east of the Jordan.

title: Song of Solomon 7:5
text:
Like Carmel; which was filled with beautiful trees and fragrant plants. 
 
  Held; fast bound with love. 
 
  Galleries; of their common palace.   Song of Solomon 1:17   But some render the word "locks."

title: Song of Solomon 7:7
text: Like to a palm-tree; majestic in height, and also fruitful.

title: Song of Solomon 7:8
text:
Go up to the palm-tree; ascend it to gather its fruits, according to the oriental custom.  The palm-tree is very lofty, with clusters of leaves and fruit at the top. 
 
vv 8-13. 
 
The excellence and glory of God's people lie in their fruitfulness. When they abound in the inward graces and outward works of righteousness, they have blessed communion with their Lord, and are safe under the banner of his love.  But when they neglect his vineyard, he will take it from them and give it to others; for he must see that it is under good culture.

title: Song of Solomon 7:9
text:
And the roof--best wine; up to this point the king speaks, then the bride takes up and completes the comparison which he has begun, and she continues her discourse to the end of the chapter.  The term "beloved" is applied only to the bridegroom. 
 
  Causing the lips--to speak; through the loveliness of their dreams. This is said to show its enlivening power.  Spiritually applied, it denotes the quickening and animating nature of the mutual love that exists between Christ and his people.

title: Song of Solomon 7:11
text: The field--the villages; where our gardens and vineyards lie.  They go forth to attend to their welfare, that is, to cultivate together the fruits of righteousness.

title: Song of Solomon 8:1
text:
As my brother; the bride expresses in these words her desire for the most intimate union with her beloved. 
 
  Should not be despised; as when separated from thee.   Song of Solomon 5:7  The presence and favor of her beloved would protect her from insult and injury. 
 
Christ's presence in his church makes her secure from injury, and honorable in the eyes of the world.

title: Song of Solomon 8:2
text:
Into my mother's house; compare  Song of Solomon 3:4 . 
 
  Who would instruct me; or, "Thou wouldest instruct me;" her beloved is also her teacher.

title: Song of Solomon 8:5
text:
Cometh up from the wilderness; a new scene here opens.  The bride is again seen coming out of the wilderness, that is, out of a state of weakness, barrenness, and depression. 
 
  I raised thee up; roused thee up, called forth thy love.  Here the spouse begins an address to her beloved, as is plain in the original Hebrew. 
 
  Under the apple-tree; the apple-tree in the spiritual garden of Zion.  One of its choice trees here represents the whole garden.  By a beautiful allegory the heavenly Bridegroom is represented as born in the garden of the church, and there also the bride wins his love.  See note on  Song of Solomon 3:11 . 
 
God's people have no strength of their own, but their strength is in Christ.  "While they by faith lean upon him, they are confirmed against all doubts, fears, dangers, difficulties, and temptations, and by union with him made partakers of all grace and comfort."

title: Song of Solomon 8:6
text:
A seal; a signet-ring, which is the symbol of inseparable union and solicitous care.   Jeremiah 22:24 Haggai 2:23  
 
  For love is strong as death; she pleads for this on the ground of his unconquerable and jealous love towards her. 
 
Nothing is so strong as the love of Christ for his people.  It overcomes all hinderances, and brings them safe home to heaven through floods of temptation within, and distress and persecution without.  Romans 8:35-39

title: Song of Solomon 8:8
text:
We have a little sister; this seems not to be the Shulamite, who has all along been represented as in full maturity, but her younger sister.  She corresponds to the "younger brother,"  Luke 15:12 , and the "other sheep which are not of this fold."   John 10:16  that is, the Gentiles who are to be called into the fold of Zion. 
 
  She hath no breasts; they are not yet grown to maturity; she is not yet ready for her espousals. 
 
Jewish saints prayed by anticipation for the gathering of the Gentiles to Christ.  Gentile Christians should, in turn, pray for the restoration of Israel to their own Messiah.

title: Song of Solomon 8:9
text: If she be a wall--if she be a door; the meaning seems to be, To whatever she be likened, we will strengthen and ornament her accordingly.  In other words, Christ will see that the gentile church is in due time adorned and strengthened with all the graces of his Spirit.  The reference is to a city wall, and to the door of a palace.

title: Song of Solomon 8:10
text:
I am a wall; the speaker is probably the gentile church anticipating her maturity, through what Christ shall do for her. 
 
  Like towers; upon the city wall. 
 
  Then; when she had reached maturity.

title: Song of Solomon 8:11
text:
Solomon; the heavenly Solomon.  Compare  Isaiah 5:1-2 Matthew 21:33 . 
 
  Unto keepers; those to whom Christ commits the interests of his church, are the keepers.  These are to bring to their Lord the worth of the fruit in money.  Compare  Matthew 21:34 Matthew 21:43 .

title: Song of Solomon 8:12
text:
My vineyard; the vineyard of the spouse.  Spiritually applied, she is the same as the keepers in the preceding verse. 
 
  A thousand--two hundred; while the keepers render to their Lord the appointed tribute, he grants them a reward for their services. 
 
While we render to God the fruits of his vineyard in their season, he will abundantly refresh our own souls by his grace, and make them "like a watered garden," full of the precious fruits of righteousness.

title: Song of Solomon 8:13
text:
Dwellest in the gardens; the words of the bridegroom to his spouse. 
 
  The companions; his fellows.  See note on  Song of Solomon 5:1 .

title: Song of Solomon 8:14
text: Make haste; the bride's parting response. See note on  Song of Solomon 2:17 .

title: Isaiah 1:1
text:
The vision of Isaiah--kings of Judah; this is the general title of the whole book.  Particular titles are prefixed to many of its sections, but it is not probable that these are arranged in exact chronological order. 
 
  Vision; prophetic revelation, with which are mingled historical descriptions of the past and reproofs for present sins. 
 
  Judah and Jerusalem; these are the great theme of the book.  Other nations come into the view only as their history is connected with that of God's people.  In "Judah and Jerusalem" was embosomed the true church of God, which had the promise of perpetual and universal dominion under the sceptre of David and his seed; and a large part of these prophecies have their complete fulfilment only in her history under Christ the Son of David. 
 
  Uzziah; he reigned fifty-two years, from about 810 to 758 before Christ. 
 
  Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah; the reign of these three kings includes a period of sixty-one years.

title: Isaiah 1:2
text: Our obligations to God our heavenly Father, are infinitely higher than to earthly parents.  For this reason, rebellion and ingratitude towards him are more heinous than the same sins committed against them.

title: Isaiah 1:4
text: Corrupters; of themselves,  Judges 2:19 , or of their way,  Genesis 6:12 .

title: Isaiah 1:5
text:
Why should ye be stricken; of what avail would it be? 
 
  Ye will revolt; notwithstanding all the stripes inflicted upon you. 
 
  Head--heart; of the nation compared to a person. 
 
  Sick--faint; from the blows already inflicted to no purpose.  This idea is amplified in the following verse.  The number of stripes inflicted shows the desperate wickedness of the people. 
 
When repeated and heavy judgments fail to reform nations or individuals, their wickedness is desperate and their destruction near.

title: Isaiah 1:8
text:
The daughter of Zion; Zion herself, as the metropolis of the kingdom.   Isaiah 37:22  
 
  Left; left remaining amid the desolation. 
 
  Cottage--lodge; a temporary hut or booth, built to shelter a keeper.  The point of resemblance is its loneliness.

title: Isaiah 1:9
text:
A very small remnant; of pious persons. 
 
God often spares wicked nations from utter destruction, for the sake of the pious remnant that is found in them.

title: Isaiah 1:10
text: When men in high places sin openly, it is the duty of God's ministers to rebuke them in a bold and fearless manner.

title: Isaiah 1:11
text:
I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs; God has no pleasure in sacrifices, except as they express the faith and obedience of the offenders. 
 
vv. 11-17 
 
God abhors the multiplication of outward services, when the heart is full of wickedness, and the life of rebellion and iniquity.  All who would render to him acceptable offerings must begin by putting away their sins.

title: Isaiah 1:12
text: To tread my courts; literally to trample--to profane them by hollow and hypocritical services.

title: Isaiah 1:13
text:
Bring no more vain oblations; God forbids not the offerings prescribed in the law, but the bringing of them with hearts full of iniquity and hands full of blood. 
 
  I cannot away--the solemn meeting; or, "I cannot bear iniquity and a solemn meeting," that is, together.

title: Isaiah 1:16
text: Wash ye, make you clean; in all such precepts we are to understand an inward cleansing of the heart, with a corresponding outward cleansing of the life.

title: Isaiah 1:17
text: Seek judgment; diligently pursue justice.

title: Isaiah 1:18
text:
Shall be as white as snow; that is, if you will thus repent and amend your ways.  The cleansing of the soul from sin includes both forgiveness and sanctification, which can never be separated from each other. 
 
To those who sincerely repent of their sins and come to God through Christ, his grace and mercy have no limits.  He will pardon the most guilty, and sanctify the most polluted.  "Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift!"

title: Isaiah 1:19
text: vv. 19-20 God's almighty power nad truth are pledged to give prosperity to the righteous, and to destroy the wicked.  The welfare of his friends and the destruction of his enemies are as certain as his own existence.

title: Isaiah 1:21
text:
vv. 21-24 
 
Wicked rulers, who oppress and rob the people, and pervert justice for gain, may be above all human power, but God will hold them responsible at his tribunal, and punish them in such a way that it shall be seen and acknowledged that he is "the Judge of all the earth."

title: Isaiah 1:22
text: Mixed with water; adulterated with water by those who sell it. They had degenerated from the piety of their forefathers.

title: Isaiah 1:23
text: Come unto them; come before them; they refuse to hear it.

title: Isaiah 1:25
text:
Purge away thy dross--take away all thy tin; from the adulterated silver, and thus restore it to its original purity.  The meaning is explained in the following verse. 
 
vv. 25-28 
 
The terrible judgments of God, by which he destroys the wicked, conduce to the purification and renewed prosperity of the true "Israel of God."

title: Isaiah 1:27
text:
With judgment--with righteousness; by the manifestation of God's righteous judgments upon the wicked.  This is the constant doctrine of the prophets.  The reference here is to the wicked in Zion. 
 
  Her converts; the remnant who survive these judgments and turn to God.

title: Isaiah 1:29
text:
Oaks--gardens; where idolatrous rites were practised.  Isaiah 57:5 Isaiah 65:3  
 
vv. 29-31 
 
The earthly objects to which sinners give their confidence, and for the sake of which they depart from the living God, not only disappoint them, but prove the occasion of their destruction.

title: Isaiah 1:30
text: Ye shall be as an oak--as a garden; since the people have sinned against God under oaks and in gardens, he will make them like withered oaks and parched gardens.

title: Isaiah 1:31
text:
The strong; the man of rank and power. 
 
  The maker of it; rather, "his work;" that is, the idol which he has made, and in which he puts his trust.  This shall set him on fire and destroy him. 
 
  Both; the strong man and his work.

title: Isaiah 2:1
text: The word that Isaiah--saw; the prophecy revealed to him in vision. This is the title of a particular section, extending through chapter 4.

title: Isaiah 2:2
text:
vv 2-4. 
 
  And it shall come to pass; these verses are found in  Micah 4:1-3  with but little variation.  The two prophets lived at the same time.  Micah 1:1   In Micah, this prophecy stands in connection with the preceding and following context.  Here it stands by itself, a bright picture before a dark scene, which however ends in glory. Isa 4.2-6 
 
  In the last days; an indefinite indication of the distant future. 
 
  The mountain of the Lord's house; Zion, including Moriah, on which the temple stood. 
 
  In the top of the mountains--above the hills; where all the earth can behold it. 
 
  Shall go forth the law; God shall sit in Zion as a lawgiver for all nations. 
 
  Judge among--rebuke; judge between them as umpire.  Thus wars will become unnecessary.  The passage is a prophecy of the extension of the true religion, from Jerusalem as a centre, over all the earth.  It plainly belongs to the Christian dispensation, but is veiled under the form of Judaism, according to which the people of God literally went up from all quarters to worship God in Jerusalem. 
 
God's infinite power, faithfulness, and love are pledged to give to his Son "the heathen for his inheritance and the uttermost parts of the earth for his possession;" so that in the darkest times his servants can labor for his cause with the assurance of final and complete success.

title: Isaiah 2:4
text: In its spirit and principles the gospel is opposed to war, injustice, and oppression of every kind; and its universal prevalence will bring to all nations perpetual peace, harmony, and blessedness.

title: Isaiah 2:5
text: O house of Jacob; in this exhortation the prophet adds, as it were, his "Amen" to the glorious prediction.

title: Isaiah 2:6
text:
Replenished from the east; filled with superstitious and idolatrous practices coming from the east.  Syria and Assyria seem to be especially intended.  Compare  II Kings 16:10 . 
 
  Please themselves; or, "abound." 
 
  Children of strangers; foreigners whom they have willingly introduced, and whose idolatrous practices they follow. 
 
When God's people seek deliverance from the troubles which their own sins have brought upon them, by allying themselves to the men of this world, and following their evil ways, they only involve themselves in deeper misery and ruin.

title: Isaiah 2:7
text: Horses--chariots; a foreign custom forbidden to the Hebrew kings.  Deuteronomy 17:16   Some understand the horses and chariots of their eastern allies.

title: Isaiah 2:9
text: Boweth down--humbleth himself; before his idols.  But the same words are, in  Isaiah 2:11 , translated, "shall be bowed down," "shall be humbled," and so in  Isaiah 2:17 .  The verse may be rendered, The man of low rank shall be bowed down, and the man of high rank shall be humbled; and do not thou forgive them.

title: Isaiah 2:10
text:
The rock--the dust; clefts of the rocks and caverns, to which the people were accustomed to flee before an invading army.  The words contain a prophecy of impending judgments. 
 
vv. 10-17 
 
Before God's judgments, the mightiest nations are weak as a little child.  Upon the high in power and place, who have been leaders in rebellion against God, they fall with irresistible force, and grind them to powder.

title: Isaiah 2:11
text: In that day; the day of God's vengeance upon the wicked; the same as "the day of the Lord," in the following verse.

title: Isaiah 2:13
text:
vv 13-16. 
 
  Cedars--pictures; the various objects enumerated in these verses denote generally all that in which the people put their delight and confidence.

title: Isaiah 2:18
text: The end of all God's judgments is the purification of his people from their sins, and their restoration to communion with himself and fruitfulness to his service.

title: Isaiah 2:20
text: Cast his idols; cast them away in his flight into dark holes.

title: Isaiah 2:22
text:
From man; from confidence in man. 
 
  Breath is in his nostrils; who is frail and short-lived. 
 
They who trust for deliverance and salvation to man, instead of God, meet with speedy and utter disappointment.

title: Isaiah 3:1
text:
For behold, the Lord-- doth take away; the reason is here given why the people should cease from confidence in man. 
 
  The stay and the staff; every kind of stay, including men and means in the widest sense. 
 
When God would chastise a nation for its sins, he very commonly takes away its able and faithful men, and gives it up to the dominion of the weak and the wicked.

title: Isaiah 3:4
text: Children--babes; unworthy and incompetent men.

title: Isaiah 3:5
text: The people shall be oppressed; this verse describes the confusion that follows from having for their rulers children and babes.

title: Isaiah 3:6
text:
When; in the time of this confusion and distress. 
 
  Thou hast clothing; decent raiment, such as a ruler is required to wear.  These words show how deep and general is the prevailing poverty. 
 
vv. 6-8 
 
Sin long persisted in, amidst God's warnings and judgments, will bring the mightiest nation to degradation and distress.

title: Isaiah 3:7
text: A healer; a binder up of the state, in its broken and ruined condition.

title: Isaiah 3:9
text: The show of their countenance; its bold and shameless look.

title: Isaiah 3:12
text:
They which lead thee--destroy the way of thy paths; place in it, as it were, stumbling-blocks and pitfalls; that is, hinder the people from walking in the right way, and thus destroy them. 
 
vv. 12-15 
 
All rulers, civil and spiritual, are entrusted with authority for the good of the people.  When they abuse their power by leading the people into error, and by oppressing and spoiling the weak, God himself will execute judgment upon them.

title: Isaiah 3:14
text:
Ancients; elders, that is, rulers. 
 
  Vineyard; put figuratively for the Lord's people committed to their care.

title: Isaiah 3:15
text: Grind the faces of the poor; either, grind their persons, that is, crush them; or, grind their faces upon the ground, by trampling them under foot.

title: Isaiah 3:16
text:
Making a tinkling; with the ankle-bands attached to their feet. Isa 3.18  These were perhaps set with small bells. 
 
vv. 16-26 
 
Female vanity and luxury are offensive to God.  The contribute largely to the corruption of morals and the decline of vital religion, and God will punish them with exemplary severity.

title: Isaiah 3:18
text:
vv 18-24. 
 
  Bravery; show or splendor. 
 
  Round tires; ornaments for the head resembling the moon in shape. 
 
  Chains; or pendants. 
 
  Mufflers; a species of veil consisting of two parts, the one thrown back over the head, the other hanging down in front, with a space between for the eyes. 
 
  Ornaments of the legs; ankle-chains, passing from one ankle-band to the other, so as to produce a short, mincing step.  They are still used in the East. 
 
  Tablets; or, smelling-boxes. 
 
  Wimples; that is, hoods or veils; better, perhaps, robes. 
 
  Crisping-pins; for the hair.  Most commentators render the original word purses. 
 
  Glasses; portable mirrors. 
 
  Burning; from exposure to the sun, or perhaps from disease.  Some of the terms in these verses are of uncertain meaning, nor is it essential that we should know their exact form and use.  They all pertained to female luxury and vanity.

title: Isaiah 3:25
text: Thy men; Jerusalem is addressed.

title: Isaiah 4:1
text:
In that day; in the day of the calamities foretold at the close of the preceding chapter. 
 
  Seven women--our reproach; the men have fallen in war,  Isaiah 3:25 , so that the surviving women cannot find husbands.  Seven women ask from one man the privilege of being called each his wife, and voluntarily offer to resign all the usual advantages of that relation. 
 
  Take away our reproach; the reproach of being unmarried and childless, which the Hebrew women regarded as a great calamity.  Genesis 29:32 Genesis 30:1 I Samuel 1:6-8 Psalms 113:9  
 
God governs the world for the good of his church, and his most terrible judgments have for their end her purification and enlargement.  In the darkest times we should not despond, but rather comfort ourselves with the assurance that they will in due time usher in a bright and joyous day for all that love Christ.

title: Isaiah 4:2
text:
In that day; in the day of these judgments, including also the period that follows them.  We are not to inquire here after a simple exact date.  The prophecy belongs to that class which have a progressive fulfilment.  Its immediate reference probably was to the Babylonish captivity, which ended in the purification of the people from idolatry, and their restoration under Ezra, Nehemiah, and others. But it covered also "the great and terrible day of the Lord." Joe 2.31, when Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans, as well as the mighty judgments yet to come, the final issue of which shall be the triumph of Christ's kingdom over all the earth. 
 
  The Branch of the Lord; the Messiah.  See note on  Isaiah 11:1 ; and  Jeremiah 23:5 Jeremiah 33:15 Zechariah 3:8 Zechariah 6:12 .  It is not, however, the person of the Messiah alone, apart from his body the church; but the Messiah in his church as her Head, and the author of all her fruitfulness, both before and after his advent.  For this reason God calls the church herself, as united to Christ, "the branch of my planting."   Isaiah 60:21 ; compare  John 15:1-7 . 
 
  The fruit of the earth; that is, of the promised land where the Messiah should appear. 
 
  Them that are escaped; that escaped these judgments.

title: Isaiah 4:3
text: Written among the living; the living, are the "escaped of Israel."  Isaiah 4:2  To be written among them is to belong to their number.

title: Isaiah 4:4
text:
Blood of Jerusalem; blood-guiltiness. 
 
  Spirit of judgment--burning; the Holy Spirit, operating in and through judgments which, like fire, purify while they destroy.

title: Isaiah 4:5
text:
A cloud and smoke by day--fire by night; as of old, when Israel came out of Egypt.   Exodus 13:21  
 
  Upon all the glory; over all Zion, now rendered glorious in holiness.   Isaiah 4:3  
 
  A defence; the defence of the cloud by day and fire by night.

title: Isaiah 5:1
text:
Will I; the prophet.
